# The economic question {.section-slide}

## Visa design links worker choice and government competition {#question .emphasis-slide}

### Countries compete through the opportunities they offer migrants

- Workers choose among offers with different fees, eligibility conditions and rights.
- Employers influence recruitment, sponsorship and the jobs migrants can take.
- Governments design offers while anticipating workers’ choices and other countries’ policies.

[Our contribution: a global visa Atlas linked to domestic and international careers.]{.fg}

# Data: pathways and job histories {.section-slide}

## The Atlas describes the pathways available to migrants {#atlas}

### Compare each pathway for a given migrant profile and year

- **Pathways:** work, study, family, protection, business and investment.
- **Terms:** eligibility, fees, sponsorship, work and family rights, duration and settlement.
- **Unit of analysis:** one pathway for a given **origin × destination × occupation × education × year**.

The same migrant may face several pathways with different requirements and rights.

:::

Family/study routes may allow work; labels alone do not define rights. Category classification needs validation.

## Job histories reveal domestic and international mobility {#histories}

### People can change employers, occupations and countries

| People and jobs in the database | Job changes in 2010–2025 |
|:--|:--|
| **549.7 million** people | **892.2 million** domestic job changes |
| **1.766 billion** jobs | **83.65 million** international job changes |

One person can change jobs several times, move abroad and later return or move to a third country.

Job locations describe where a person works; residence and citizenship require separate information.

Positions are not completed job spells. A same-country job transition is not same-job staying.

# Demand, costs and visa design {.section-slide}

## Workers choose among accessible visa pathways {#worker-demand}

### Fixed geography and government-chosen offers

$$
u_{ijt}=\textcolor{#EE7733}{\alpha\log\widetilde w_{ijt}}
+\underbrace{\textcolor{#0077BB}{\beta' z_{od}}}_{\text{fixed geography}}
+\underbrace{\textcolor{#EE7733}{\gamma' q_{jt}}}_{\text{chosen visa terms}}
+\xi_{jt}+\varepsilon_{ijt},\qquad j=(d,v).
$$

$$
p_{ijt}(C_{it})=
\frac{\mathbf 1\{j\in C_{it}(\textcolor{#EE7733}{r_t})\}\exp(V_{ijt})}
{\sum_{k\in C_{it}(\textcolor{#EE7733}{r_t})}\exp(V_{ikt})}.
$$

- **Net wage** $\widetilde w$: earnings net of taxes and fees on a common horizon.
- $\textcolor{#0077BB}{z}$: fixed geography; $\textcolor{#EE7733}{q}$: rights; $\textcolor{#EE7733}{r}$: eligibility.
- $C_{it}(r_t)$ includes staying and the worker’s accessible pathways.

Migration RUMs: [@kennanEffectExpectedIncome2011].

::: {.nav}
[Denominators and MPML](#mpml){.button} [Fixed effects](#fixed-effects){.button} [Preference versus access](#demand-identification){.button} [Return: conclusion](#next-steps){.button} [Return: literature careers](#literature-careers){.button}
:::

::: {.notes}
Illustrative static RUM, not an adopted or estimated individual likelihood. Worker i starts in origin o; j=(destination d, pathway v); t is time. V is utility excluding the idiosyncratic shock. Conditional logit requires iid type-I extreme-value shocks conditional on the relevant set and observables. Staying is normalised as alternative0 with its own utility, not assigned a foreign visa. Net earnings must be positive for the log; fees are annualised or converted to a common consumption horizon, not subtracted as a lump sum from an annual flow without conversion. Fixed distance is treated as predetermined in this model, not an instrument for every policy. q includes portability, duration and family rights; r sets eligibility and affects C. Actual access can also depend on sponsorship, admission and information. Legal compatibility is not complete access. Revelio normally reveals destination job country, not visa route: route probabilities must be aggregated over v before matching country flows. Dynamic migration RUMs are precedents, not this static formula verbatim. ξ is unobserved destination/pathway attractiveness. Wages/net fees and chosen characteristics may respond to it.
Application charges paid before an uncertain admission decision belong to the application stage when that uncertainty matters; they are not automatically equivalent to a deduction from earnings conditional on entry. The net-wage term is a common-horizon illustration, not a maintained identification of those stages.
:::

## Estimation must separate preferences from access {#cost-preliminaries}

### Gravity links choices to flows; access creates selection

$$
\mu_{odt}=N_{ot}\sum_v \mathbb E[p_{i,dv,t}(C_{it})\mid o,t].
$$

**Two endogenous margins:** $\widetilde w_{ijt}$ and $q_{jt}$ may covary with $\xi_{jt}$; the accessible set $C_{it}$ is partly unobserved.

$N_{ot}$ is the population at risk; movers alone do not identify it.

- **Offers:** demand inversion and instruments [@berryNonparametricIdentificationDifferentiated2024].
- **Access:** latent or restricted choice sets [@agarwalDemandAnalysisLatent2025; @almagroChoicesConstraintsDisentangling2026].
- **Information:** revealed-preference bounds [@porcherMeasuringInformationFrictions2025].

::: {.nav}
[Fixed effects and samples](#fixed-effects){.button} [Monetary comparability](#monetary){.button} [Government costs](#government-costs){.button}
:::

::: {.notes}
No current gravity estimates are presented. N_ot is the origin population at risk and μ is expected flow; expectation averages worker heterogeneity and accessible sets. The expression is an aggregation identity conditional on the illustrative choice model, not a claim that a generic heterogeneous RUM reduces to a linear PPML index. Standard logit/gravity restrictions can supply an aggregate starting point. A zero observed cell can reflect an unavailable route, an unaffordable offer, low preferences, a finite-sample zero or measurement/coverage; never classify every zero as selection. Even positive flows face endogenous characteristics: governments choose rules and rights in response to latent attractiveness/composition, while firms and governments affect wages or net charges. These are distinct from predetermined geography. Destination-time and dyad fixed effects can absorb policy or distance, respectively, rather than identify them automatically. PPML handles count zeros but does not by itself identify unavailable alternatives. Berry–Haile supplies conditional identification/instrument restrictions; Agarwal–Somaini addresses latent choice constraints; Almagro–Sood is a housing comparator with its own set restrictions; Porcher etal separates information frictions and preferences through revealed-preference bounds. These are candidate routes, not an already solved estimator for visa data.
:::

## Governments choose visa policies as the supply side {#government-supply}

### Governments anticipate worker choices and rival offers

$$
M_d^*\in\arg\max_{M_d\in\mathscr M_d}G_d(M_d,M_{-d}^*).
$$

- **Menu $M_d$:** eligibility, rights and fees; $\mathscr M_d$ contains feasible policies.
- **Payoff $G_d$:** resident welfare and political support; recruitment, fee receipts and real costs shape the welfare component.
- **Competition:** a country’s offer changes workers’ alternatives to rival destinations.

Political-economy benchmark: *Protection for Sale* [@grossmanProtectionSale1994].

::: {.nav}
[Government objectives](#government-costs){.button} [Welfare](#welfare){.button} [Conclusion](#next-steps){.button}
:::

::: {.notes}
Adapted from the PhD Review slide Visa:competing contracts under policy change, with its best-response condition. M_d is a country's feasible menu, and G_d is evaluated at worker choices induced by all menus. A unilateral deviation holds rival menus fixed but allows workers to choose again. Grossman–Helpman1994 supplies a proposed political-economy starting point: government welfare plus political contributions, with organised interests choosing contribution schedules. Transferring that mechanism to visas requires specifying relevant domestic groups, their schedules and information; exclusive worker destination choice alone is not the original common-agency game. Lobbying data and government weights are not identified here. Resident-welfare accounting includes fiscal effects net of real costs; fee receipts must not be counted twice. This is a proposed supply-side research step, not an estimated equilibrium or a completed application of Protection for Sale.
:::

## Conclusion and next steps {#next-steps}

### Visa pathways connect policy design to workers’ careers

- The number of work pathways has increased.
- Pathways combine different eligibility conditions, costs and rights.
- About half of domestic and international job changes involve occupational switching.

#### Next steps

- Continue demand estimation, separating preferences from access.
- Develop a supply-side model of governments’ visa-policy choices.

Three descriptive findings, followed by two next research steps. Occupational switching is event-weighted, not a fraction of distinct people. Growth is the recorded work-pathway series and coded occupation/education passes on fixed support. Neither statement establishes complete legal availability or a causal policy effect.
:::

# Appendix: legal offers and data {.section-slide}

## Connecting legal offers with global career allocation {#contribution .literature}

### Route-level policy bundles connect policy measurement with worker histories

- **Policy measurement and competition:** legal regimes select different migrants and compete for talent [@helblingMeasuringImmigrationPolicies2017; @dehaasGrowingRestrictivenessChanging2018; @czaikaGravityHighSkilledMigration2017; @shacharRaceTalentHighly2006].
  - **Our contribution:** a broad motive inventory and dated, work-oriented route bundles for comparable profiles.
- **International allocation:** migration choices reallocate talent across countries and over careers [@bertoliMultilateralResistanceMigration2013; @brinattiThirdCountryEffectsUS2024; @amanzadehReturnMigrationHuman2024; @bhalothiaGlobalValueCities2025; @pratoGlobalRaceTalent2025].
  - **Our contribution:** connect legal menus to domestic and international career transitions.
- **Legal options and labour markets:** access to migrant labour, employer restrictions and connected domestic markets shape firm and worker outcomes [@doranEffectsHighSkilledImmigration2022; @townsendHowRestrictingMigrants2025; @borusyakUnderstandingMigrationResponses2026].
  - **Our contribution:** cross-country legal-menu measurement, with competing government offers as a proposed extension.

::: {.nav}
[Full literature map](#literature-map){.button} [Demand identification](#demand-identification){.button} [Government objectives](#government-costs){.button} [Return: question](#question){.button}
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not claim the first policy dataset, third-country response, or visa-induced employer-mobility result. Townsend–Allan concerns within-destination employer options and wage setting; Borusyak et al. domestic region–industry responses under specified shocks. Neither supplies a ready international coefficient or closure. The competing-government model remains a research extension. Cai–Lin–Szeidl is intentionally excluded from this presentation.
:::

## A migrant’s profile determines the relevant visa menu {#bridge}

### Match the person, destination and year to the pathway

| Profile | Visa requirements | Job histories |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Year** | Rules applying in that year | Job and move dates |
| **Occupation** | Occupation-specific conditions | Type of work before and after a move |
| **Origin** | Nationality or residence conditions | Previous job country; nationality is matched separately |
| **Education** | Required qualifications | Highest reported degree |

## Governments offer access, costs and rights {#motivation .compact}

### Admission is one part of a package that shapes a person’s future options

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
#### Access to employment

- Occupation, citizenship and sponsorship can determine which routes a worker can use.
- Employer portability changes the jobs available **after admission**.
- A route opening can redirect workers from another destination rather than create a new move.
:::
::: {.column width="49%"}
#### Residence and membership

- Family work rights, renewal and settlement change the value of the initial offer.
- Argentina’s investment-linked **citizenship** initiative illustrates a different membership instrument—not a work visa.
- Announced terms, binding rules and operational access are distinct.
:::
::::

## Occupational groups are not a skill ladder {#skills}

- SOC major groups describe kinds of work; their numeric codes are not ranks.
- The broad SOC-to-ISCO reference scenario permits upward, downward and equal changes for about **95%** of events.
- Routine/non-routine, cognitive/manual and preparation requirements are distinct concepts.
- A defensible skill-transition matrix needs a verified finer code/vintage and a declared crosswalk; it cannot be recovered from destination skill marginals.

[The occupation matrix is descriptive evidence. A ranked skill matrix is not yet established.]{.fg}

# Appendix: estimation and literature {.section-slide}

## Demand estimates depend on the available alternatives {#mpml}

### Counts and shares depend on the choice set

$$
\mu_{ra}=\exp(\alpha_r+\beta x_{ra}+z_{ra}'\gamma),\quad
p_{ra}=\frac{\exp(\beta x_{ra}+z_{ra}'\gamma)}{\sum_{b\in A_r}\exp(\beta x_{rb}+z_{rb}'\gamma)}.
$$

- Profiling the row effect gives the corresponding Poisson objective on **identical support and weights**.
- The alternatives in $A_r$, including staying, must be defined for the question.
- PPML can include observed count zeros; access restrictions still need a model.

::: {.nav}
[Return: worker responses](#worker-demand){.button}
:::

::: {.notes}
The conditional likelihood is ell(beta,gamma)=sum_{r,a}Y_{ra}log p_{ra}. Poisson profiling and conditional multinomial objectives coincide on identical support and weights. Estimating a model on positive policy-matched international cells does not itself supply the missing population at risk, stayers, applications or legal availability. No current fitted coefficient is presented here.
:::

## Fixed effects determine the monetary comparison {#fixed-effects .compact}

### The variation left after conditioning determines what can be estimated

| Specification | Conditional row | Additional fixed effects |
|:--|:--|:--|
| L | Origin × year | Destination; occupation × education × year; dyad |
| D | Origin × year | Destination × year; occupation × education × year; dyad |
| T | Origin × occupation × education × year | Destination × year; dyad × occupation |
| K/E | Type-specific origins | Destination × occupation(× education) × year; dyad × occupation |

K/E absorb the monetary policy variation: **not identified**, not an estimated zero effect.

The estimand and fixed effects must leave the relevant policy variation. Dyad effects absorb fixed distance; destination-time effects absorb destination-wide offers. Neither automatically resolves individual access restrictions.

::: {.nav}
[Return: worker responses](#worker-demand){.button} [Return: monetary preliminaries](#cost-preliminaries){.button}
:::

## Rich histories do not by themselves separate preferences from access {#demand-identification .compact .alert-slide}

### Observed choices combine preferences with constraints on available options

[@berryNonparametricIdentificationDifferentiated2024; @agarwalDemandAnalysisLatent2025]

- Legal compatibility, consideration, sponsorship, admission and take-up are distinct stages.
- Observed characteristics and repeated choices add information; they do not eliminate market-level unobservables or supply excluded variation automatically.
- Applications, refusals, route-linked admissions and usable offers can help distinguish these stages.

**Our task:** define the choice occasion, population, support and policy variation before treating conditional allocation slopes as migrant elasticities.

::: {.nav}
[Return: contribution](#contribution){.button} [Return: worker responses](#worker-demand){.button}
:::

## Fee competition identifies a net marginal object {#government-costs .compact}

### Recovering separate benefits and costs requires additional restrictions

$$
G_d=f_d'n_d(f)+B_d(n_d)-C_d(n_d),\qquad
c_d-b_d=f_d+(D_d^{\mathsf T})^{-1}n_d.
$$

$D_d$ is the own-route quantity-by-fee derivative matrix; $b_d$ and $c_d$ are marginal benefits and resource costs.

- Requires identified unilateral fee responses, matching fee/quantity units, interior optimality and no omitted binding constraint.
- Capacity adds a multiplier; application fees need application-stage revenue.
- Adding the same function to $B_d$ and $C_d$ leaves choices unchanged: unrestricted benefits and costs are **not separately identified**.

Trade-policy inversion provides a comparison, not a Visa identification theorem [@adaoWorldTradingSystem2025].

::: {.nav}

:::

## Welfare needs a population and an adjustment mechanism {#welfare}

### Who is affected depends on the scope of the counterfactual

- Migrants and families; origin residents; destination residents; employers; governments.
- Wages, amenities, fiscal effects and housing or other prices may adjust.
- Fees are transfers, waiting uses time, and restrictions can remove future options.
- Government recruitment gains do not establish gains for everyone affected.

**Counterfactual scope:** first hold other offers fixed, then allow market adjustment and government responses under explicit assumptions.

:::

## Policy measurement and allocation frame the contribution {#literature-map .literature .literature-detail}

### Previous findings and the contribution to each literature

- **Policy measurement:** levels, signed changes and instrument indicators have different units [@helblingMeasuringImmigrationPolicies2017; @dehaasGrowingRestrictivenessChanging2018; @czaikaGravityHighSkilledMigration2017].
  - **Our contribution:** dated route bundles and comparable occupation–education profiles.
- **Alternative destinations:** multilateral resistance and third-country diversion already have direct treatments [@bertoliMultilateralResistanceMigration2013; @brinattiThirdCountryEffectsUS2024].
  - **Our contribution:** connect changing legal menus to domestic and international careers.
- **Careers and equilibrium:** dynamic location choice; employer options and wage setting; connected domestic markets [@kennanEffectExpectedIncome2011; @townsendHowRestrictingMigrants2025; @borusyakUnderstandingMigrationResponses2026].
  - **Our contribution:** cross-country legal-menu measurement, with government and employer responses as proposed extensions.
- **Identification and policy:** constrained demand and revealed policy objectives require setting-specific restrictions [@berryNonparametricIdentificationDifferentiated2024; @agarwalDemandAnalysisLatent2025; @adaoWorldTradingSystem2025].
  - **Proposed extension:** identify worker substitution before recovering government incentives under explicit restrictions.

::: {.nav}
[Return: contribution](#contribution){.button} [References](#references){.button}
:::

## Career histories have close empirical precedents {#literature-careers .literature}

### Professional trajectories, place values and policy-induced location choices

- **Return and onward careers:** professional histories trace return migration and foreign experience [@amanzadehReturnMigrationHuman2024].
  - **Our contribution:** connect those trajectories to dated legal-route measurement, not claim the first use of onward histories.
- **Place and human capital:** employment histories reveal conditional place premia and allocation patterns [@bhalothiaGlobalValueCities2025].
  - **Our contribution:** measure the legal offers and constraints facing comparable profiles.
- **Policy and founding location:** a start-up visa changes entrepreneurs’ location choices [@leeEffectImmigrationPolicy2023].
  - **Our contribution:** a broader route/history mapping rather than one programme or corridor.

::: {.nav}
[Return: contribution](#contribution){.button} [Demand framework](#worker-demand){.button}
:::

## Screening and causal gravity inform different steps {#literature-methods .literature}

### Mechanism recovery, information timing and policy-effect identification

- **Inverse screening:** allocations, transfers and outside-option restrictions can identify types and costs [@aryalIdentificationEstimationMultidimensional2024].
  - **Proposed use:** specify what visa choices must reveal before interpreting an inferred government cost.
- **Sequential screening:** information timing and regularity shape multidimensional menus [@gaoMultidimensionalSequentialScreening2026].
  - **Proposed use:** formalise which worker attributes and signals are known when a route is offered or chosen.
- **Causal gravity:** staggered policy effects require comparison and aggregation assumptions [@nagengastStaggeredDifferenceinDifferencesGravity2025].
  - **Proposed use:** distinguish policy-effect identification from structural demand or government-objective recovery.
